item.title: index
item.dc:creator: Honey Orser
item.description:
Introduction

My exploratory analysis in this blog focuses on the event scheduling dynamics of the Milano-Cortina 2026 Olympics, as I am aiming to understand how the Olympic Games are structured – ranging from the number of events across different sport disciplines to the temporal distribution of medal awarding events and the typical time commitments required for various types of event sessions.

For my exploration, I am looking at Milano-Cortina 2026 Winter Olympics Data, which consits of observations of 21 variables, and contains structured data about the Olympics schedule, events, and venues across all included sport disciplines.

I am investigating three questions of interest in my analysis of the Milano-Cortina 2026 Winter Olympics schedule data:

  • Which sport disciplines have the most events scheduled, and of those, what proportion are dedicated to training versus live competition?

  • How are medal events distributed across the Olympic calendar – are they evenly distributed?

  • What is the typical duration of different types of Olympic events, and does this duration vary based on whether the event is for training, awarding medals, or live competition?

To answer these questions, I am focusing on the six variables – discipline_name, is_training, is_medal_event, date, start_datetime_local, and end_datetime_local.

When interpreting the following visualizations, it is important to note that events in the context of this data set refer to scheduled sessions, not necessarily a single race. For example, one Ice Hockey event might be one 3 hour session that covers one game, while one Alpine Skiing event might cover dozens of individual runs.

Visualizations

most_events <- schedule |>
  mutate(training_ind = if_else(is_training == TRUE, "Training", "Competition")) |>
  group_by(discipline_name, training_ind) |>
  summarise(n_events = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(discipline_name = fct_reorder(discipline_name, n_events, .fun = sum))

ggplot(data = most_events, aes(x = discipline_name, y = n_events, fill = training_ind)) +
  geom_col(position = "stack", color = "midnightblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = NULL,
       y = "Number of Events",
       title = "Events per Discipline",
       fill = "Event Type") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Training" = "midnightblue",
                               "Competition" = "mintcream"))

This visualization reveals that Curling, Freestyle Skiing, and Ice Hockey are the disciplines with the most scheduled events at the 2026 Winter Olympics, with Curling having the highest number of events by about 200. Only some disciplines have official training sessions, indicated by the dark blue sections of the bars. These disciplines include Bobsleigh, Luge, Ski Jumping, Alpine Skiing, Skeleton, and Nordic Combined.

training_props <- schedule |>
  mutate(training_ind = if_else(is_training == TRUE, "Training", "Competition")) |>
  group_by(discipline_name, training_ind) |>
  summarise(n_events = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(discipline_name) |>
  mutate(total_discipline_events = sum(n_events)) |>
  filter(training_ind == "Training") |>
  mutate(prop_training = n_events / total_discipline_events) |>
  select(discipline_name, prop_training) |>
  arrange(desc(prop_training))

kable(training_props)
discipline_name prop_training
Luge 0.6422018
Bobsleigh 0.6101695
Skeleton 0.5714286
Nordic Combined 0.4000000
Ski Jumping 0.3448276
Alpine Skiing 0.2941176

The above table shows the breakdown of proportion of training events for disciplines which have them scheduled, highlighting that Luge, Bobsleigh, and Skeleton disciplines have over half of their scheduled events as official training sessions.

medal_events_dist <- schedule |>
  filter(is_medal_event == TRUE) |>
  count(date)

ggplot(data = medal_events_dist, aes(x = date, y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "mintcream", color = "midnightblue") +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), vjust = -0.5) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 day", date_labels = "%d %b %Y") + 
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Date",
       y = "Number of Medal Events",
       title = "Distribution of Medal Events Across Days of the Olympics") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, vjust = 1, hjust = 1))

This visualization tracks the frequency of medal events across the 2026 Winter Olympics calendar. It reveals a buildup in the competition schedule; the olympic games begin with a relatively quiet opening period dominated by preliminaries, eventually leading into high-density peak days from February 8th through February 20th, and finally slowing down with a quiet ending period during the last days as the games draw to a close.

events_duration <- schedule |>
  
  mutate(duration_mins = as.numeric(difftime(end_datetime_local, 
                                             start_datetime_local,
                                             units = "mins")),
         event_type = case_when(
           is_medal_event ~ "Medal",
           is_training ~ "Training",
           TRUE ~ "Competition"
         )) |>
  filter(!is.na(duration_mins), duration_mins > 0)

ggplot(data = events_duration, aes(x = event_type, y = duration_mins)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.3, color = "midnightblue", fill = "mintcream") +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.7, color = "midnightblue", fill = "mintcream") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Event Type",
       y = "Duration (minutes)",
       title = "Typical Duration of Different Types of Olympic Events") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

This visualization compares the time commitments of different event categories, revealing that Competition and Medal events are generally longer and less variable than Training sessions. While training sessions tend to be tightly clustered around a standard 60-to-120-minute window, competition and medal events show much longer spreads, indicating a broader range of durations. Notably, the Medal category has the lowest median duration and narrowest spread, suggesting that award ceremonies have an objective process and are relatively straight forward. However, there are some outliers in the Medal category, indicating that some award ceremonies take much longer, potentially due to extended flower presentations and/or athelte interviews.

Conclusion

While my three visualizations provide a strong overview, there are some inherent limitations to my approach with this data. Treating every row as one event is potentially misleading because one Ice Hockey event could consist of one game, whereas one Alpine Skiing event could consist of several individual runs. Another potential flaw is that my analysis relies on local_datetime. If certain events were recorded using different offsets or if there were data entry errors in the end_datetime_local leading to 0-minute durations, they were filtered out, potentially ignoring valid but poorly formatted data points.

With more time and/or additional data sets, I would expand my exploratory analysis to look at weather impact on events. Winter sports are very reliant on weather conditions such temperature, wind, and snow. I would be interested in comparing the schedule with climate data for the Milano and Cortina regions to see if I could predict which, if any, events are at risk for scheduling delays or cancellations.

Connection to Class Ideas

  • My visualizations use appropriate geometric objects (geoms) to match the data types of questions of interest. I used bar charts (geom_col) for the number of scheduled events and distribution of medal events because bar charts are best for comparing magnitudes and frequencies across categories over time. I used violin olots and boxplots to show the density and variance of typical time duration for different types of events.

  • My Events per Discipline visualization utilizes fct_reorder. In class, we learned that alphabetical sorting is rarely the most informative choice. By reordering the sport disciplines by the total number of scheduled events, I am using spatial positioning to immediately highlight the disciplines with the highest number of events, allowing readers to identify trends much more quickly.

item.title: Big Tech Stock Prices
item.dc:creator: Honey Orser
item.description:
Introduction

In this blog, I am looking at the Big Tech Stock Prices data set (originally sourced from Kaggle), which is a comprehensive collection of the daily stock prices and volume of 14 different tech companies, including Apple, Amazon, and Meta. The data details how these tech giants fared from 2010 to 2022.

My exploration is based around on the idea of risk vs. reward, and centers on the question: Which tech stocks are the most volatile, and how do their daily price distributions differ? To answer this, I am focusing on three primary variables:

  • adj_close is the closing price after adjustments for all applicable splits and dividend distributions, which I use to track the baseline value of the stocks.

  • open and close are the the price at market open and the price at market close (adjusted for splits), respectively, and I use them to calculate the daily percentage fluctuations that define volatility.

  • stock_symbol represents the full name of the associated company, which I need to group and compare trends and happenings across the companies in the data set.

This is a fairly large data set, containing 45,088 observations. An important contextual note for the reader is that all companies have 3,271 prices, excepting Meta which has 2,688, and Tesla which has 3,148 because they were not publicly traded for part of the period examined in the data.

Visualizations

ggplot(data = big_tech_stock_prices, aes(x = date, 
                                         y = adj_close, 
                                         color = stock_symbol)) +
  geom_line(show.legend = FALSE) + 
  facet_wrap(~stock_symbol) +
  labs(title = "Big Tech Stock Performance Over Time",
       subtitle = "Tracking adjusted closing prices.",
       x = "Year",
       y = "Adjusted Closing Price ($)",
       caption = "**Figure 1:** This time-series analysis uses the *adj_close* variable to
                  track appreciation across 14 tech companies.") +
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(plot.caption = element_markdown()) +
  scale_color_paletteer_d(palette = "vapeplot::vaporwave")

This visualization contextualizes the reward component of my analysis. By plotting the adj_close price, the resulting visual shows the actual wealth generated for stockholders over time (adjusted for all applicable splits and dividend distributions).

Readers should notice that while the Big Tech stock market sector is often referenced as a whole, the growth trajectories of companies within the sector are actually very different. A key observation is the difference in trend stability; some companies maintain a steady and reliable trend of capital appreciation, while other companies show much more fluctuation with massive vertical spikes followed by corrections*. This visualization shows that all tech stocks don’t behave the same way; it’s the specific stock, not the general sector, that determines whether investors experience consistent gains or extreme volatility over time.

*Note: Stock market corrections are generally defined as a drop in value of 10% or more from recent market highs.

daily_return_data <- big_tech_stock_prices |> 
  mutate(daily_change = ((close - open) / open) * 100,
         abs_daily_change = abs(daily_change))
ggplot(data = daily_return_data, aes(x = stock_symbol,
                                     y = daily_change,
                                     fill = stock_symbol)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = 1, show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~stock_symbol, scales = "free") +
  labs(title = "Daily Return Distributions by Stocks",
       subtitle = "Outliers represent extreme market days.",
       x = NULL,
       y = "Daily Return (%)",
       caption = "**Figure 2:** This plot illustrates daily price volatility where the central
       boxes represent typical behavior and the outliers identify shocks.") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
        plot.caption = element_markdown()) +
  scale_fill_paletteer_d(palette = "vapeplot::vaporwave")

To look at daily risk, I use faceted boxplots to visualize the distribution of daily returns (the percentage change from open to close). This visualization reveals the internal stability of these stocks. Each boxplot shows the range of a company’s typical daily gain or loss; the central boxes show where the price usually settles and the outliers represent extreme trading days. These are moments where the stock price moved significantly more than usual, indicating which companies are more prone to sudden price shocks.

The key takeaway here is the consistency of the stock: a more compact box indicates a stable, predictable asset, while a wider box with a lot of outliers identifies a stock prone to sudden fluctuations in price. Readers should note that the scales for each panel are not the same across the grid – they are relative to each individual boxplot.

sector_median <- median(daily_return_data$abs_daily_change, na.rm = TRUE)
ggplot(data = daily_return_data, aes(x = fct_reorder(stock_symbol, abs_daily_change),
                                     y = abs_daily_change,
                                     fill = stock_symbol)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = 1, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = sector_median, 
             linetype = 2, 
             color = "red4", 
             size = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Volatillity Ranking: Daily Price Fluctuations",
       x = "Stock Symbol",
       y = "Absolute Daily Return",
       caption = "**Figure 3:** This comparative ranking uses the *fct_reorder* function to
       sort tech companies by their median absolute daily return.") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.caption = element_markdown()) +
  scale_fill_paletteer_d(palette = "vapeplot::vaporwave")
Warning: Using `size` aesthetic for lines was deprecated in ggplot2 3.4.0.
ℹ Please use `linewidth` instead.

This final plot defines the risk ranking by sorting these companies based on their median absolute daily returns. The dashed line represents the sector median, marking the middle point of volatility for this group of companies to provide a clear point of reference for comparison.

This visualization should enable readers to identify the sector’s stable points versus its more unpredictable points. Stocks further to the right of the dashed line (sector median) are objectively more volatile than others more to the left, so they require a higher risk tolerance. This ranking helps investors to see exactly where a company like Tesla (TSLA) or NVIDIA is on a scale of risk compared to established companies like Microsoft (MSFT) or Google (AAPL).

Conclusion

A potential flaw in my exploration is that I used to calculate the daily return variable, but this only accounts for what happens with prices from open to close . The formula doesn’t consider what happens with prices when the market is closed, which could be significant.

With additional data and more time, I would be interested in including additional data to support and contextualize the the adjusting closing price trends. This could include relevant news, social media mentions, and other supporting data that might help explain what else was going on during extreme market days (outliers in Figures 2 and 3) and why they happened.

Connection to Class Ideas

  • Data-to-Ink Ratio: I aimed to minimize data-to-ink ratio in my visualizations by making the plots simple but informative, so they are better remembered and more enjoyable for viewers.

  • Appropriate Color Scales: I used a qualitative color scale to distinguish between companies because they are unordered categories.
